sentences.text:
Respondent No.1 - State of Madhya Pradesh by Shri Adity  Government Advocate appearing on behalf of the Advocate General  None appears for respondent No.2 - Jayesh Vyas S/o Mr.
 Laxminarayan Vyas.

ORDER The present petition has been preferred under Section 528 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, whereby the petitioner seeks quashment of FIR No.0354/2024 dated 21.10.2024 registered at Police Station M.G. Road, Indore, District Indore (MP) for offences punishable under Sections 420, 406 and 34 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 (IPC) insofar as the said FIR relates to the present petitioner.

2. The brief facts of the case are that the petitioner is the wife of the principal accused, namely, Mr.
Kapil Goyal.

As per the prosecution case, the alleged date of incident is 07.08.2023, whereas the First Information Report NEUTRAL CITATION NO. 2026:MPHC-IND:45 2 MCRC-4758-2025 was registered much later on 21.10.2024 at Police Station Mahatma Gandhi Road, District Indore,
bearing Crime No. 354/2024.
3.
The said FIR has been lodged by the complainant against two accused persons, namely, Mr. Kapil Goyal and the present petitioner, Smt. Deepali Goyal.

The allegations levelled by the complainant against both the accused are that they cheated him of an amount of 2,00,00,000/- by preparing and using forged documents purportedly relating to a housing finance company, and by manipulating such documents, thereby committing the alleged offence of cheating.
On the basis of the aforesaid allegations, the present FIR has been registered against the petitioner and the co-accused, Mr. Kapil Goyal.

sentences.text: As per the allegations emanating from the FIR, the dispute is founded upon a financial transaction alleged to have taken place between the father of respondent No. 2 and the husband of the petitioner.
It is alleged that a loan amount of 2,00,00,000/- was advanced in August, 2023 to the husband of the petitioner for investment purposes.
It is further alleged that a non-registered loan agreement was executed between the said parties and certain post-dated cheques were handed over as security.
5. It is alleged that due to business losses, only a part of the loan amount could be repaid and the remaining amount was not returned within the stipulated period.
Consequent thereto, proceedings under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 were initiated with respect to the dishonour of cheques.

6. During the pendency of the aforesaid proceedings, the impugned NEUTRAL CITATION NO.
2026:MPHC-IND:45 3 MCRC-4758-2025 FIR came to be lodged alleging offences under Sections 420, 406 and 34 of IPC.
The present petitioner has been arrayed as an accused on the premise that her bank account details allegedly appeared in a document purportedly forwarded by a third person to the complainant.

7. Notably, the FIR does not allege that the petitioner was a party to the loan agreement, that she received any portion of the loan amount, or that she made any representation or inducement to the complainant or his father at any point of time.

8. Learned counsel for the petitioner contended that the entire dispute is purely civil in nature arising out of a loan transaction and that the petitioner has been falsely implicated merely because she is the wife of the principal accused.
It was submitted that none of the essential ingredients of Sections 406 or 420 of IPC are satisfied insofar as the petitioner is concerned.

9. It was further submitted that there is no allegation of entrustment of property to the petitioner,
nor is there any allegation of dishonest intention or inducement at the inception of the transaction attributable to her.
Invocation of Section 34 of IPC was also assailed on the ground that there is no material indicating any common intention or participation by the petitioner.
10. Learned Government Advocate appearing for the respondent/State opposed the petition and submitted that the FIR discloses cognizable offences and that the investigation is still in progress.
It was argued that the Court should be slow in interfering at the threshold.

It is NEUTRAL CITATION NO. 2026:MPHC-IND:45 4 MCRC-4758-2025 pertinent to take note of the fact that the respondent No.2 has been duly served, but has not marked his presence neither in person nor through any counsel.
11. This Court has bestowed its anxious consideration to the rival submissions and has meticulously perused the FIR and the material placed on record.
12. The jurisdiction under Section 528 BNSS ( pari materia to Section 482 CrPC) is intended to prevent abuse of the process of law and to secure the ends of justice.

The Supreme Court in State of Deepali Goyal vs The State Of Madhya Pradesh on 29 December, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/162671912/
2 Haryana v. Bhajan Lal, 1992 Supp (1) SCC 335 , has authoritatively held that criminal proceedings can be quashed where the allegations, even if taken at their face value, do not constitute any offence or where the proceedings are manifestly attended with mala fides.

sentences.text: 13. In the present case, the genesis of the dispute is admittedly a loan transaction.
The FIR itself reveals that the loan was advanced to the husband of the petitioner and the grievance of the complainant essentially pertains to non-repayment of the said amount.

14. The offence of criminal breach of trust under Section 406 of IPC is founded upon "entrustment"
of property.

The Supreme Court in S.W. Palanitkar v. State of Bihar , (2002) 1 SCC 241 , and Satishchandra Ratanlal Shah v. State of Gujarat , (2019) 9 SCC 148 , has categorically held that a mere loan transaction does not amount to 'entrustment' and that breach of a contractual obligation,
without 'entrustment', cannot give rise to criminal breach of trust.

entities.text: S.W. Palanitkar v. State of Bihar , (2002) 1 SCC 241
entities.label: PRECEDENT

entities.text: Satishchandra Ratanlal Shah v. State of Gujarat , (2019) 9 SCC 148
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: NEUTRAL CITATION NO. 2026:MPHC-IND:45 5 MCRC-4758-2025 15.
In the case at hand, there is not even a whisper in the FIR suggesting that any property was entrusted to the present petitioner.
In the absence of this foundational ingredient, the offence under Section 406 IPC cannot be sustained against her.
16. For constituting an offence of cheating, dishonest intention at the inception of the transaction is sine qua non .

The Supreme Court in Hridaya Ranjan Prasad Verma v. State of Bihar , (2000) 4 SCC 168 , has drawn a clear distinction between mere breach of contract and the offence of cheating,
holding that failure to keep a promise subsequently cannot be presumed to be cheating unless fraudulent intention is shown at the inception.

entities.text: Hridaya Ranjan Prasad Verma v. State of Bihar , (2000) 4 SCC 168
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: 17. The FIR does not disclose any act of inducement, misrepresentation or deception on the part of the petitioner at the beginning of the transaction.
Mere inability to repay a loan or subsequent default, howsoever blameworthy, does not ipso facto constitute the offence of cheating.

18. The Supreme Court in Vesa Holdings Pvt. Ltd. v. State of Kerala, (2015) 8 SCC 293 , has cautioned that criminal law should not be used to settle scores arising out of purely civil disputes,
particularly in commercial and financial transactions.
19.

entities.text: Vesa Holdings Pvt. Ltd. v. State of Kerala, (2015) 8 SCC 293
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: Invocation of Section 34 IPC requires prima facie material to establish common intention and participation.

The Supreme Court in Nagaraja v. State of Karnataka , (2009) 14 SCC 703 , has held that mere association or relationship with the principal accused is not sufficient to attract Section 34 IPC, in the absence of meeting of minds.

entities.text: Nagaraja v. State of Karnataka , (2009) 14 SCC 703
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: NEUTRAL CITATION NO. 2026:MPHC-IND:45 6 MCRC-4758-2025 20.
In the present case, no material has been placed on record to indicate that the petitioner shared any common intention with the principal accused or participated in the alleged acts.
Mechanical invocation of Section 34 IPC is, therefore, wholly unsustainable.

sentences.text: The facts of the present case unmistakably indicate that the criminal machinery has been set in motion to exert pressure in a loan dispute.

22. That even if the prosecution case is accepted in its entirety as it stands, the two essential ingredients of the offence punishable under Section 420 of the Indian Penal Code--namely,
dishonest intention at the inception and deception from the very beginning--are not made out.

From the material available on record, it prima facie appears that the present petitioner has been falsely implicated, not on account of any overt act attributable to her, but merely to exert pressure upon her husband.
The manner in which the petitioner has been arrayed as an accused clearly indicates a mala fide attempt, and her implication in the present case appears to be wholly unwarranted.
23. That the prosecution case, even if taken at its face value, does not disclose the essential ingredients of the offence punishable under Section 406 of IPC.
The essential ingredients of Section 406 IPC, as defined under Section 405 IPC, necessarily require entrustment of property and dishonest misappropriation or conversion of the same.
In the present case, there is no NEUTRAL CITATION NO. 2026:MPHC-IND:45 7 MCRC-4758-2025 entrustment of any property.

The prosecution has failed to establish even prima facie that the petitioner had any dominion or proprietary interest over the alleged property or that any amount was ultimately used by the petitioner for his personal benefit.
Consequently, the basic ingredients of Section 405 IPC, and in turn Section 406 IPC, are conspicuously absent from the entire charge-sheet.
Similarly, no prima facie case is made out so as to attract the essential ingredients of the offence under Section 420 IPC.
In the absence of these foundational elements, the continuation of the criminal proceedings would amount to an abuse of the process of law and, therefore, the same deserve to be quashed.
24. Allowing such proceedings to continue against the petitioner would result in grave injustice and would amount to abuse of the process of law, which this Court is duty-bound to prevent.
25. In view of the aforesaid discussion, this Court is of the considered opinion that no prima facie case is made out against the present petitioner.
26. Accordingly, the petition is allowed.

FIR No.0354/2024 dated 21.10.2024 registered at Police Station M.G. Road, Indore, District Indore (MP), for offences punishable under Sections 420, 406 and 34 of the IPC is hereby quashed insofar as it relates to the present petitioner.
